pontic-olbia.name: Pontic Olbia
pontic-olbia.summary: An ancient Greek city on Ukraine's Southern Bug estuary, founded in the 7th century BC by colonists from Miletus, that traded grain, fish and slaves on the Black Sea.

miletus.name: Miletus
miletus.summary: Ancient Greek city on Anatolia's western coast, a wealthy maritime and trading power that founded dozens of Mediterranean and Black Sea colonies and was home to early philosophers such as Thales; known in Hittite records as Millawata.

satyrus-i.name: Satyrus I
satyrus-i.summary: Spartocid ruler of the Bosporan Kingdom from 432 to 389 BC who expanded his father's foreign policy, conquered Nymphaion, besieged Theodosia, and strengthened ties with Athens.

ammianus-marcellinus.name: Ammianus Marcellinus
ammianus-marcellinus.summary: A Roman soldier and historian (c. 330–391/400) whose Latin history, the Res gestae, chronicled Rome from 96 to 378 CE, though only the section from 353 to 378 survives.

history-of-crimea.name: Cherronesus
history-of-crimea.summary: An ancient Greek name for the Crimean Peninsula, also known as Tauris or the Tauric Chersonese, settled by Greek colonists from around the 5th century BCE.

strabo.name: Strabo
strabo.summary: Greek geographer (64/63 BC to about 24 AD) best known for his Geographica, a descriptive survey of the peoples and places known in his time.

chersonesus.name: Chersonesus
chersonesus.summary: An ancient Greek colony founded around the 6th century BC on Crimea's coast, later known in medieval Greek as Cherson; it operated for a time as a democracy and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

pantikapaion.name: Panticapaeum
pantikapaion.summary: An ancient Greek city founded by Milesians on the eastern shore of Crimea in the late 7th or early 6th century BC; its ruins now lie within modern Kerch.

tovsta-mohyla.name: Tovsta Mohyla
tovsta-mohyla.summary: Ancient Scythian burial mound in southern Ukraine where a solid 24-carat gold pectoral and other treasures were discovered in 1971.

ionia.name: Ionia
ionia.summary: An ancient region on the central western coast of Anatolia settled by Greek Ionians, home to twelve cities of the Ionian League and central to conflicts between Persia and Greece.

darius-the-great.name: Darius the Great
darius-the-great.summary: Third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire (522–486 BCE), who ruled it at its territorial peak, reorganized it into provinces, and commissioned the Behistun inscription.

scythians.name: Scythians
scythians.summary: An ancient Eastern Iranic nomadic people who migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe in the 9th-8th centuries BC, dominating the region through mounted warfare before being conquered by the Sarmatians in the 3rd-2nd centuries BC.

agathyrsi.name: Agathyrsi
agathyrsi.summary: An ancient Scythian-culture people who lived near the Sea of Azov before being pushed into the Transylvanian Plateau, known mainly from Herodotus's 5th-century BC account.

cimmerians.name: Cimmerians
cimmerians.summary: An ancient Iranic nomadic people from the Pontic-Caspian steppe who migrated into West Asia, known mainly through Assyrian and later Greek and Roman records.

pontic-caspian-steppe.name: Pontic–Caspian Steppe
pontic-caspian-steppe.summary: A vast grassland stretching from the northern Black Sea to the Caspian Sea, corresponding to ancient Scythia and Sarmatia, and thought to be where horses were first domesticated.

alans.name: Alans
alans.summary: Ancient Iranian-speaking nomadic people who migrated to the North Caucasus and later parts of Europe and North Africa, related to the Sarmatians and first recorded by Roman sources in the 1st century CE.

huns.name: Huns
huns.summary: A nomadic people from Central Asia who built a short-lived empire on Rome's Danube frontier by 430 CE, launching devastating raids under King Attila until his death in 453.

goths.name: Goths
goths.summary: A Germanic people first recorded in the 3rd century CE north of the Danube, whose migrations and 378 victory over Rome at Adrianople helped bring about the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

battle-of-adrianople.name: Battle of Adrianople
battle-of-adrianople.summary: A battle fought on 9 August 378 near Adrianople in Thrace, in which Gothic rebels under Fritigern won an overwhelming victory over the Eastern Roman army and killed Emperor Valens, an event often marking the start of Rome's fall.

philip-ii-of-macedon.name: Philip II of Macedon
philip-ii-of-macedon.summary: King of Macedon from 359 to 336 BC who built up its military power, defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC, and was the father of Alexander the Great.

lysimachus.name: Lysimachus
lysimachus.summary: Thessalian officer and successor of Alexander the Great (c. 360–281 BC) who became king of Thrace, western Asia Minor and Macedon, before being defeated and killed by Seleucus in 281 BC.

getae.name: Getae
getae.summary: Ancient people who lived along the Lower Danube in what is now Bulgaria and Romania, closely related to the Thracians and Dacians, first recorded resisting a Persian invasion in 513 BC.

sarmatians.name: Sarmatians
sarmatians.summary: A confederation of nomadic Iranian horse peoples who dominated the Pontic steppe from about the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD, later clashing and allying with Rome and the Goths.

idanthyrsus.name: Idanthyrsus
idanthyrsus.summary: A Scythian king of the 6th century BCE who faced an invasion of his country by the Persian Achaemenid Empire.

herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

constantine-the-great.name: Constantine the Great
constantine-the-great.summary: Roman emperor from 306 to 337, the first to convert to Christianity, who legalized Christian worship across the empire and founded Constantinople as its new capital.

aoric.name: Aoric
aoric.summary: A 4th-century Thervingian Gothic king, son of Ariaric and father of Athanaric, raised in Constantinople where a statue honored him.

ariaric.name: Ariaric
ariaric.summary: A 4th-century pagan ruler of the Thervingian Goths who, after heavy losses in a campaign led by Constantine the Great's son, was forced to sign a treaty with Rome in 332.

naqsh-e-rostam.name: Naqsh-e Rostam
naqsh-e-rostam.summary: An ancient necropolis near Persepolis in Iran holding rock-cut tombs of four Achaemenid kings, including Darius the Great and Xerxes, with later Sasanian reliefs nearby.

j-nos-harmatta.name: János Harmatta
j-nos-harmatta.summary: Hungarian linguist (1917–2004) who deciphered Parthian ostraca and papyri of Dura-Europos and was first to decipher a major Bactrian inscription.

ionian-revolt.name: Ionian Revolt
ionian-revolt.summary: A rebellion of Greek cities in Asia Minor against Persian rule (499–493 BCE), triggered by dissatisfaction with Persian-appointed tyrants and marked by the burning of Sardis in 498 BCE.

filippovka-kurgans.name: Filippovka kurgans
filippovka-kurgans.summary: A group of burial mounds north of the Caspian Sea in Russia's Orenburg region, dated to about 450-300 BC and marking a transition between Sauromatian and Sarmatian cultures.

eusebius.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
eusebius.summary: Historian and bishop of Caesarea from about 314, known as the 'Father of Church history' for works including the Ecclesiastical History and a life of Emperor Constantine.

ovid.name: Ovid
ovid.summary: A Roman poet (43 BC – AD 17/18) ranked with Virgil and Horace, best known for the Metamorphoses, who was exiled by Augustus to the Black Sea for the rest of his life.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Founder of the Roman Empire, ruling as its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, and known earlier as Octavian.

exile-of-ovid.name: Carmen et error
exile-of-ovid.summary: Latin for 'a poem and a mistake,' the vague explanation the Roman poet Ovid gave for his banishment from Rome to Tomis in 8 AD, whose true cause remains uncertain.

ulfilas.name: Ulfilas
ulfilas.summary: A 4th-century Gothic bishop of Cappadocian Greek descent who converted the Goths to Christianity and devised the Gothic alphabet to translate the Bible into Gothic.

gothic-alphabet.name: Gothic alphabet
gothic-alphabet.summary: An alphabet created in the 4th century by bishop Ulfilas to translate the Bible into Gothic, based mainly on Greek letters with some Latin and Runic influence.

gothic-language.name: Gothic (language)
gothic-language.summary: An extinct East Germanic language spoken by the Goths, known mainly from a 6th-century copy of a 4th-century Bible translation and the earliest Germanic language attested in sizeable texts.

dacian-language.name: Dacian (Getic) language
dacian-language.summary: An extinct, poorly documented language believed to be Indo-European, spoken in ancient Dacia; only one inscription survives, with a small number of words reconstructed from plant and personal names.

tristia.name: Tristia
tristia.summary: A collection of poems in elegiac couplets written by Ovid during his first years of exile from Rome to Tomis on the Black Sea, after his banishment in AD 8.

epistulae-ex-ponto.name: Epistulae ex Ponto
epistulae-ex-ponto.summary: A work by the Roman poet Ovid in four books of verse letters describing his exile in Tomis, composed around AD 12–13 and addressed to his wife and friends.

codex-argenteus.name: Codex Argenteus
codex-argenteus.summary: A 6th-century illuminated manuscript containing a 4th-century Gothic translation of the Bible's gospels, mostly held today in Uppsala, Sweden.

gothic-bible.name: Gothic Bible
gothic-bible.summary: The Bible translated into the Gothic language, traditionally credited to bishop Wulfila in the 4th century, though likely the work of a team of translators.

scythia.name: Scythia
scythia.summary: A geographic region of the ancient Graeco-Roman world covering the Pontic steppe, home to the Scythians, an ancient Eastern Iranic nomadic people.

auxentius-of-durostorum.name: Auxentius of Durostorum
auxentius-of-durostorum.summary: A bishop of Durostorum, also probably known as Mercurinus, who as an Arian was prominently in conflict with St Ambrose.

ambrose.name: Ambrose
ambrose.summary: Bishop of Milan from 374 to 397 and an influential Roman theologian, later counted among the four Great Latin Church Fathers.

bosporan-kingdom.name: Bosporan Kingdom
bosporan-kingdom.summary: An ancient Greco-Scythian state in eastern Crimea and the Taman Peninsula, later a long-lasting Roman client kingdom whose wealth came from exporting wheat, fish and slaves.

kingdom-of-pontus.name: Kingdom of Pontus
kingdom-of-pontus.summary: A Hellenistic kingdom on the Black Sea coast of northern Anatolia, founded in 281 BCE and ruled by a Persian-descended dynasty, reaching its height under Mithridates VI before Rome's conquest in 63 BCE.

nero.name: Nero
nero.summary: Roman emperor from AD 54 to 68, the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, remembered for orchestrating his mother's murder and for scandalous public performances as actor and musician.

tiberius-julius-cotys-i.name: Tiberius Julius Cotys I
tiberius-julius-cotys-i.summary: Roman client king of the Bosporan Kingdom, active in the mid-first century AD (around 45 to 63 AD).

oium.name: Oium
oium.summary: A name for Scythia, roughly in modern Ukraine, where the Goths settled under legendary King Filimer after leaving Gothiscandza, according to a 6th-century chronicle.

zalmoxis.name: Zalmoxis
zalmoxis.summary: A divinity of the Getae and Dacians described by Herodotus before 425 BC; later writers called him a philosopher and linked him to Pythagoras.

jordanes.name: Jordanes
jordanes.summary: 6th-century Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent turned historian, whose Getica is one of only two surviving ancient works on early Gothic history.

getica.name: Getica
getica.summary: Latin work written by Jordanes around 551 CE, the only surviving detailed ancient account of the origin and history of the Goths.

deceneus.name: Deceneus
deceneus.summary: A priest and adviser to the Dacian king Burebista in the 1st century BCE, described as second in power to the king, later credited with 'civilizing' the Getae.

anacharsis.name: Anacharsis
anacharsis.summary: A Scythian prince and philosopher of uncertain historicity who lived in the 6th century BC.

seven-sages-of-greece.name: Seven Sages of Greece
seven-sages-of-greece.summary: An honorary title given to seven philosophers, statesmen and lawgivers of the 7th to 6th centuries BCE, renowned for their wisdom.

burebista.name: Burebista
burebista.summary: King of the Getae and Dacian tribes from 82/61 BC to 45/44 BC, the first to unify the Dacian tribes, who expanded the kingdom through conquest before clashing with Rome.

attila.name: Attila
attila.summary: Ruler of the Huns from 434 until his death in 453, known as "the Scourge of God," who invaded the Balkans, Gaul and Italy but never took Rome or Constantinople.

sword-of-attila.name: Sword of Mars
sword-of-attila.summary: A legendary sword said to have been carried by Attila the Hun, also called the Sword of Attila or Sword of God.

porphyry-of-tyre.name: Porphyry
porphyry-of-tyre.summary: A Phoenician Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305) who edited his teacher Plotinus's works and wrote an introduction to logic used throughout the Middle Ages.

cynicism-philosophy.name: Cynics
cynicism-philosophy.summary: Followers of Cynicism, an ancient Greek philosophy holding that happiness comes from living simply and virtuously, free of social convention; its most famous figure was Diogenes.

lucian.name: Lucian
lucian.summary: Hellenized Syrian satirist and rhetorician (c. 125–after 180) known for tongue-in-cheek writings mocking philosophers and superstitions, written in Greek though his native language was probably Syriac.

rhyton.name: Rhyton
rhyton.summary: A cone-shaped drinking or pouring vessel, often shaped like an animal's head or horn, used across ancient Eurasia from the Bronze Age onward, especially from Persia to the Balkans.

aphrodite-urania.name: Aphrodite Urania
aphrodite-urania.summary: An epithet of the Greek goddess Aphrodite representing a 'heavenly' or spiritual aspect of love, distinct from purely physical love.

sauromatian-culture.name: Sauromatian culture
sauromatian-culture.summary: An Iranic Iron Age culture of horse nomads living between the lower Volga River and the southern Ural Mountains, roughly the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, known only from camps and large burial mounds.

chernyakhov-culture.name: Chernyakhov culture
chernyakhov-culture.summary: An archaeological culture that flourished from the 2nd to 5th centuries AD across what is now Ukraine, Romania, Moldova and Belarus, a mix of Gothic, Geto-Dacian and Sarmatian peoples that declined after the Hunnic invasion.

dacians.name: Dacians
dacians.summary: The ancient Indo-European-speaking people of Dacia, near the Carpathians and west of the Black Sea, closely related to the Getae and often grouped with the Thracians.

srubnaya-culture.name: Srubnaya culture
srubnaya-culture.summary: An Iranic Late Bronze Age culture (1900–1200 BCE) in the eastern Pontic-Caspian steppe, successor to the Yamnaya culture and generally linked to early Iranian speakers.

andronovo-culture.name: Andronovo culture
andronovo-culture.summary: A group of related Late Bronze Age cultures from about 2000 to 1150 BCE, spanning from the southern Urals to central Siberia and western Xinjiang, generally agreed to have been Indo-Iranian.

saka.name: Saka
saka.summary: Nomadic Eastern Iranian peoples of the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin from the 9th century BC to the 5th century AD, closely related to the Scythians.

itkul-culture.name: Itkul culture
itkul-culture.summary: An early Saka culture of the 7th to 5th centuries BCE based in the eastern Ural foothills, known for metalworking, later absorbed into the Early Sarmatian culture.

vikentiy-khvoyka.name: Vikentiy Khvoyka
vikentiy-khvoyka.summary: Czech-born Ukrainian archaeologist (1850–1914) who discovered the Neolithic Trypillia culture of Ukraine and researched several other ancient cultures, including the Scythian and Zarubintsy.

zarubintsy-culture.name: Zarubintsy culture
zarubintsy-culture.summary: An archaeological culture that flourished north of the Black Sea along the Dnieper and Pripyat rivers from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD, possibly linked to the early Slavs.

ermanaric.name: Ermanaric
ermanaric.summary: Greuthungian Gothic king who died in 376, said by some ancient and later legendary sources to have ruled a vast realm before the Hunnic invasion.

athanaric.name: Athanaric
athanaric.summary: King of several branches of the Thervingian Goths for at least two decades in the 4th century, facing invasions by Rome and the Huns; considered the first king of the Visigoths.

penkovka-culture.name: Penkovka culture
penkovka-culture.summary: An archaeological culture in Ukraine, Moldova and Romania, whose people are commonly identified with the Antes described by 6th-century Byzantine historians.

ossetians.name: Ossetians
ossetians.summary: An Iranic ethnic group native to Ossetia in the Caucasus Mountains, descended from the ancient Alans and speaking the Ossetian language.

deer-stones-culture.name: Deer stones
deer-stones-culture.summary: Bronze Age megaliths carved with images of flying deer, found mainly in Mongolia and nearby Siberia, generally placed near ancient graves and thought to guard the dead.

khwarazm.name: Khwarazm
khwarazm.summary: A large oasis region on the Amu Darya river delta in Central Asia, center of the Iranian Khwarezmian civilization until Turkic tribes took over in the 9th century.

taksai-kurgans.name: Taksai kurgans
taksai-kurgans.summary: A group of Saka or Sauromatian burial mounds in northwestern Kazakhstan dated to about 500 BCE, including the tomb of a richly adorned woman known as the 'golden lady'.
